title: Strict Majority
statement:
A value is a **strict majority** if it appears **more than half** of the time in `numbers` (for example, at least 3 times in a list of 5, at least 3 times in a list of 4).

Return the strict majority value, or `-1` if there is none. Exactly half is not enough.

examples.explanation: 3 appears 4 times out of 7, which is more than half.
Every value appears once out of four: no value appears more than twice.

hints.nudge: If a value really is more than half of the list, what happens if you cancel pairs of DIFFERENT values against each other?
hints.pattern: Boyer-Moore voting: keep one candidate and a count; same value adds a vote, a different value removes one. Then check the candidate with a second pass.
hints.pseudocode:
candidate = none; votes = 0
for x in numbers:
  if votes == 0: candidate = x
  votes += 1 if x == candidate else -1
count how many times candidate appears
return candidate if count * 2 > len(numbers) else -1
hints.walkthrough: The easy way counts every value with a hash map and checks which count is above half: O(n) time and O(n) memory. For O(1) memory use voting. Every time two DIFFERENT values meet they cancel each other out; a value that makes up more than half of the list cannot be cancelled completely, so it is what is left standing. Keep a candidate and a vote count: when the count is 0 the current number becomes the candidate; a number equal to the candidate adds one vote, any other number takes one away. The candidate is only a PROPOSAL: if no strict majority exists the loop still ends with some candidate, so count how many times it appears and compare with half the length to be sure.
